content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a contrastive prompt tuning framework that explicitly optimizes for the learned prompts to be consistent with the image space. When combined with cross-entropy loss, the contrastive loss helps learning prompts so that the model has consistent predictions across different views of an image while also maintaining the consistency of pairwise similarities among different images.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengthens:
1) The proposed regularization term in this paper helps to improve the generalization of the Prompt Tuning method.
2) The proposed method works well on the few-shot learning experimental settings, and extensive experimental results also demonstrate this .

Weaknesses:
1) The novelty is very limited, such regularization appears many times in the classification methods.
2) The proposed method encourages the model to have consistent predictions across different views of an image. Although the experimental results have been improved, It should further verify that whether the performance improvements is form the data augmentation or the proposed consistency constraint. This is very important to illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
3) The proposed regularization aims to improve the generalization capbility of the VPT model on few-shot learning. If the training examples become large (e.g., large amount of shots for each class), what will happen? This regularization may decrease the performance in such a scenario?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Overall, this paper is well written, and the main idea is clearly presented. Since the algorithm is incredibly simple, it should be very easy to be reproduced.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the novelty of this paper is very limited, and the proposed method could work well under few-shot scenarios.  This paper is well organized and easy to be understood.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes CPT, a contrastive-learning-based prompt tuning framework for vision-language models, which aims to solve the poor generalization problem caused by the cross-entropy-only training paradigm. Specifically, they propose to tune soft prompts by two additional contrastive losses: instance contrastive loss and relational consistency loss. The former encourages the prompt to learn instance discriminative features from images. The latter constrains the prompt making the logit space consistent with various inter-image semantic relationships in the image feature space. Experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that their methods outperform the previous method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength： 
1. The proposed method delivers good performance in comparison with the existing methods. 
2. The proposed method is clearly described

Weakness:
1. The proposed method is not impressive, and it is somewhat incremental. Various variants of contrastive learning have been developed for representation learning. This paper seems just migrate some existing frameworks to vision language prompt tuning and does not show some additional task-specific design or innovation. For example, [1] also utilize contrastive learning to improve the performance and generalization ability of the model, and their experiments on zero-shot setting obtain similar findings as this paper. The difference between the two papers is that [1] applies self-supervised contrastive learning to pre-training, but this paper applies it to prompt tuning. Therefore, I believe the migration from pre-training to prompt tuning is incremental and does not constitute a major contribution.

[1] Norman Mu, Alexander Kirillov, David Wagner, and Saining Xie. Slip: Self-supervision meets language-image pre-training. arXiv preprint arXiv:2112.12750, 2021.

2. The proposed two losses are the core contributions of this paper, but only one setting is used to evaluate the effect of losses, which is not convincible enough. Experiments with various baselines and more settings should be conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The authors also need to allocate more space for the ablation study of the two losses.

3. This paper only presents the results of quantitative experiments but lack some qualitative analysis.

4. Some expressions are confusing. For example, In Sec 3.2, the authors write that: “First, we apply an … such that the prompt learns to predict different views of same image (positives) similarly.” Why the prompt could “predict view.” Also, in Sec 3.2, “L_{InsCon} encourages the prompt to learn instance discriminative features from the images.” Why could the prompt “learn features” from the images. 

5. There are also some grammatical errors, e.g., “different views of same image” should be “different views of the same image”, “in few-shot setting” should be “in the few-shot setting”, “restricts generalization of learned prompts” should be “restricts the generalization of learned prompts”, etc.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I believe this work is reproducible. For “clarity, quality, novelty”, please see “Strength And Weaknesses”.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed method is effective, but its novelty is limited. The ablation study of the proposed method is not convincing enough. I am also confused about some expressions in the paper. Overall, I rate this paper marginally below the acceptance threshold.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper aims to improve the generalization in vision-language pre-training models, through ensembling contrastive learning and prompt tuning. An intra-image discriminative contrastive loss and an inter-image relational contrastive loss are added for optimization. Extensive experiments are conducted on 11 datasets, including zero-shot, few-shot, and cross-dataset scenarios.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths：
1. The paper is well organized, makes good use of space, and is easy to follow.
2. Prompting vision-language pre-training for better generalization is a trending and interesting research topic.
3. Experimental results on multiple benchmarks demonstrate decent performances.

Weaknesses:
1. Novelty: The idea is fairly trivial.  Intra-image and inter-image contrastive losses have been widely studied for pre-training represention learning or fine-tuning. Recently, prompt tuning has also been well explored. Simply ensembling these two brings few insights to the community. 

2. Method: Some designs do not seem rigorous. For the RelCon loss, why is the feature similarity matrix calculated between z1 and z3, but the logit similarity matrix is calculated between I2 and I3 (not I1 and I3)? Why use KL divergence, which is asymmetrical, to measure the distribution gap? More discussion and experiments are needed. For the InsCon loss, why views of different images are treated as negatives? Different images may belong to the same semantic category. 

3. Experiments. Some experimental evaluations are flawed and fail to adequately support the main claims. For the image stream, existing methods of prompt tuning hardly use data augmentation for performance boosts, which makes the comparisons with this paper unfair. Optimizing prompt vectors using multiple cross-entropy losses (classify one image with multiple views) is missing in ablation studies. More problematic, the gains of two contrastive losses are fairly minor (0.5-0.6%), even comparing to naive L_{CE} (without data augmentation). Since the effect of losses is crucial, the reviewer suggests to provide detailed results on all datasets and scenarios. In conclusion, it is doubtful whether contrastive learning can improve the generalization of prompt tuning. Comparing to CoCoOp, this paper shows comparable performance, through simply ensembling two learned prompts. However, such a simple ensemble has brought 1.4% average gains in Table1, which seems to be the key to improvements. How ensemble is implemented? Will the performance improve further, if more prompts are used for ensemble? Although CoCoOp needs a few more parameters (30K params are completely acceptable in reality), its processing cost (time and memory) may be lower, because data augmentation and memory buffer are not required.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The presentation of the paper is generally clear, making the paper easy to follow.
Quality: Although many experiments have been carried out, the key ablation studies are flawed and fail to adequately support the main claims. 
Novelty: The idea is fairly trivial, and the method is unremarkable.
Reproducibility: Many details are described such that an expert should be able to reproduce the main results.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper simply plugs together two methods (i.e., contrastive learning & prompt tuning), which is lack of novelty and brings few insights to the community. Although many experiments have been carried out, the key ablation studies are unfair and fail to adequately support the main claims. Therefore, I would vote for a rejection.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper argues that the conventional cross-entropy loss for prompt tuning limits the generalization capability of learned prompts. To this end, they propose Contrastive Prompt Tuning (CPT), which explicitly optimizes the learned prompts to be consistent with the image space. Specifically, CPT consists of two new contrastive learning terms. The first term helps learning prompts by encouraging the model to have consistent predictions across different views of an image, which the second term maintains the consistency of pairwise similarities among different images.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths
+ Extensive experiments have been conducted to validate the effectiveness of CPT, including four different image classification settings (seen-to-unseen classes adaption within a dataset, cross-dataset transfer, domain generalization, and few-shot classification with domain shift), and results on 15 datasets and 10 vision-language models.

## Weaknesses
+ The proposed method is quite simple. Both two new proposed contrastive losses are existing methods. It seems that there is no technique contribution in this paper.
+ Since the proposed contrastive learning is generalizable to any prompt generation strategies, it would be more convincing by incorporating the CPT into other prompt generation strategies, such as CoCoOp.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
+ Clarity: The whole paper is well-written, and easy-to-follow.
+ Novelty: The novelty is limited. Although it claimed to be the first work to integrate self-supervised contrastive learning for prompt tuning, the used techniques are off-the-shelf.
content.summary_of_the_review: The whole paper is well-written, and extensive results are conducted to validate the effectiveness of the proposed CPT. However, the new technical contributions are quite limited.

content.title: Contrastive Prompt Tuning Improves Generalization in Vision-Language Models
content.abstract: Prompt tuning, which focuses on learning continuous text prompts for adapting large vision-language models, has attracted much attention in recent years. While prior works show promising performance over the hand-crafted prompts, they typically use cross-entropy loss for learning prompts, which limits their generalization capability in many real-world scenarios. Motivated by the effectiveness of contrastive learning for improved generalization, we introduce Contrastive Prompt Tuning (CPT), an incredibly simple yet highly efficient framework that explicitly optimizes for the learned prompts to be consistent with the image space. In particular, combined with cross-entropy loss, our contrastive losses help learning prompts so that the model has consistent predictions across different views of an image while also maintaining the consistency of pairwise similarities among different images. Extensive experiments on a battery of datasets demonstrate that our proposed method significantly outperforms the existing methods in improving model's generalization, while also achieving consistent improvements in few-shot in-domain performance for a wide variety of vision-language models.
